method: Every idea is built from one real death custom, church office, river-city trade or toll law, turned into a rule the thumb can feel.

ideas.name: The Three Dues
ideas.idea: Harm is Rung (bell, knock, cry), Written (chisel, quill, notch) or Covered (earth, iron, cloth). Each risen dead was denied one rite and shows which: a gaping mouth (never rung), a blank slab on its chest (never written), no shroud (never covered). Any harm can drop it, but a body dropped by the wrong kind stands again at the next toll with 60% life; dropped by its due it is laid for good and its drop doubles. Protection is three yes-or-no states, Muffled, Blank and Shrouded, each halving one kind.
ideas.source: A decent death was owed three things: the passing bell, a name cut in stone or entered in the register, and covering earth; these dead rose for want of one.
ideas.nearest: Tabletop trolls that stay dead only if burned, and elemental weakness charts. Here the matching kind does not hit harder: it decides whether the kill is permanent, and the penalty arrives on the bell.

ideas.name: Tale, Weight and Term
ideas.idea: Harm is counted three ways: by tale (how many blows), by weight (how heavy each), by term (how long it stays). Each of the dead answers to one. Tale-bound: it falls after a set count of blows, however light: 3 for a child, 6 for a woman, 9 for a man. Weight-bound: a flat amount comes off every blow, so only heavy ones count. Term-bound: nothing harms it until the player has stood within 5 m for a set number of seconds. The player's wards are bound the same ways.
ideas.source: The Exchequer took payment by tale (counted), by weight, or held over for a term; the death knell counted nine strokes for a man, six for a woman, three for a child.
ideas.nearest: Hit-count shields, flat armour thresholds and stand-here timers each exist separately in many games. Here they are the only three protections there are, and they replace typed damage altogether.

ideas.name: In Mourning
ideas.idea: When an elite dies, every lesser dead within 8 m goes into mourning for it. Full mourning, 6 s: it turns black, stops, faces the body and will not strike. Half mourning, the next 6 s: grey, half speed, strikes half as often. Then it is out. Harming a mourner in full mourning ends its mourning at once and it strikes 30% faster for 6 s. The player chooses: walk away through a quiet crowd, or keep fighting and wake it with skills that hit areas.
ideas.source: Mourning was worn for set terms that stepped down by grade, full black and then grey half-mourning, and ordinary business stopped while it lasted.
ideas.nearest: Pacify and daze effects that break on damage. This one is caused by an important death nearby, steps down in two grades on a clock, and punishes the player for breaking it.

ideas.name: Forfeit
ideas.idea: Falls on whatever harms the player, when a skill, vow or pick says so. If the offender was moving when it struck (a charger, a thrown or rolling thing), all of it is forfeit: it changes sides for 6 s, then falls. If it was standing still, only the part that struck is forfeit: it cannot strike for 6 s but still walks and blocks. A ground patch counts as standing and goes dark for 6 s. Forfeit things give experience only if the player lays them.
ideas.source: Under the law of deodand a thing that caused a death was forfeit: if it was in motion the whole of it, if at rest only the part that struck.
ideas.nearest: Charm and disarm effects. Which of the two happens here is decided by whether the attacker was moving when it hit, so the player can choose how to be struck.

ideas.name: Coined
ideas.idea: Two coins are laid on a dead thing's eyes. For 5 s it cannot see: it keeps walking on the heading it had, in a straight line, turning only when it bumps a wall, and it strikes whatever it walks into, the other dead included. Any Rung (sound) harm within 4 m tells it where the player is and ends the state early. When the state ends the two coins drop as a pickup; if the player lays it while it is coined, four coins drop.
ideas.source: Coins were laid on a corpse's eyes to keep them shut, and were said to be the fare for the ferryman.
ideas.nearest: Blind and confuse states. This one fixes the heading instead of scrambling it, is undone by the player's own noise, and pays the player back in coin.

ideas.name: Felon
ideas.idea: One dead thing is cried as felon for 6 s. Every other dead thing within 6 m of it must turn and strike it instead of the player. If a pursuer lays the felon, that pursuer becomes the felon and the 6 s start again, up to 5 times; if the player lays the felon the cry ends. Things that cannot hear (Mutes, anything Muffled) never join and are never chosen. The player receives the experience and drops of every body the chase leaves.
ideas.source: When the hue and cry was raised everyone who heard it had to join the chase, and it was handed on from township to township.
ideas.nearest: Enrage and bait effects that turn enemies on one of their own, as in BioShock. This one passes to whoever makes the kill, so it travels through the crowd by itself until the player ends it.

ideas.name: Abjured
ideas.idea: An abjured dead thing stops fighting, takes up a cross and walks in a straight line to the nearest edge of the district, where it leaves for good and gives nothing. While it keeps to its line the player cannot harm it. If anything moves it more than 2 m off the line (a push, a pull, a body shoving it) it has strayed: it stands lost for 4 s, takes triple harm from everything, and the other dead strike at it. Laying a strayed abjurer gives triple experience.
ideas.source: A felon in sanctuary could abjure the realm: he walked barefoot with a wooden cross straight to an assigned port, and if he strayed from the road anyone might kill him.
ideas.nearest: Banish and fear effects that remove an enemy for no reward. Here the banishment is a visible straight walk that the player can spoil on purpose to turn it into a triple-value kill.

ideas.name: Sin-laden
ideas.idea: Some dead carry sins, shown as 1 to 9 dark lumps stacked on the back. Each sin gives its carrier 5% more harm and 3% less speed. When a sin-laden thing dies its sins pass to whatever is nearest within 2 m: another dead thing, or the player. The player carries sins on the same terms and sheds them only by leaving through a gate or by letting a Dole-seeker take one pickup per sin. Lay sin-carriers from a distance, or step in on purpose to take the load.
ideas.source: A sin-eater took a dead person's sins on himself by eating bread and drinking ale passed over the corpse, and was shunned for what he carried.
ideas.nearest: Stacking buffs that jump to a nearby ally on death. This one can jump to the player, is a deliberate trade of speed for harm, and is shed by custom rather than by time.

ideas.name: Named
ideas.idea: A thing that has been cried three times is Named until the next toll. Its crier's skills may pick it at any distance and through walls. In return it always knows where its crier is: it ignores hiding and mourning dress and moves 20% faster toward them. The rule cuts both ways. When a dead Crier names the player, every dead thing in the district gains that hold on the player, and the player's skills may pick that Crier from anywhere on the map.
ideas.source: The town crier proclaimed a name three times with 'Oyez', after which the person named was held to have had notice wherever they were.
ideas.nearest: Marks that reveal a target, and taunts. This is one state with the same rule for both sides: between namer and named, range and hiding stop counting.

ideas.name: Pole, Wick and Stone
ideas.idea: Three personal measures. Pole is the character's yardstick: skill reach and area are written in Poles (1 Pole is 1 m plus 1% per point). Wick is their clock: durations are written in Wicks (1 s plus 1% per point). Stone is their weight: harm per blow, and how much unbanked loot they carry before slowing, are written in Stones. Nothing has a minimum. Instead gear is cut to a measure, such as Pole 40: within 5 points of it the item fits and its properties gain 25%.
ideas.source: Old measures came from the trades: the pole or perch of land, the inch of candle that timed an auction, the stone of the market weigh-beam.
ideas.nearest: Area, duration and damage stats, and attribute requirements on gear. Here the attributes are the units the skill text is written in, and gear rewards matching a value exactly rather than exceeding it.

ideas.name: Sexton
ideas.idea: Digs the graves and rings the bell. The thumb's new verb is to stop: stand still for 2.5 s and the Sexton finishes a grave underfoot, a 2 m pit. The next 6 dead to walk into it drop in and are laid; then it closes. At most 4 graves lie open. The Sexton digs ahead of the crowd and leads it across. Starting skill, Spadeful: every 1.2 s throws grave-earth over the nearest dead within 5 m, harming it and slowing it 30% for 2 s.
ideas.source: The sexton dug the parish graves, and a grave is the one place the dead are meant to stay.
ideas.nearest: Trap-laying characters, and bonuses for standing still in some horde games. Here standing still is construction time, and what is built is a hole that fills up and closes.

ideas.name: Verger
ideas.idea: Carries the verge, the rod that clears the way for a procession. While the Verger walks, a wedge 3 m long opens ahead: dead inside it are shouldered 1.5 m to either side and cannot strike for 0.5 s. The thumb drives straight through the thickest crowd instead of round it. The wedge exists only while moving and covers only the front 120 degrees, so stopping or turning back inside a crowd is fatal. Starting skill, The Verge: every 0.9 s raps the two dead nearest the wedge's edges.
ideas.source: A verger walked ahead of the procession with a rod of office to clear people and animals out of its way.
ideas.nearest: Charge and plough abilities on a cooldown. Here parting the crowd is the class's ordinary walk, and the price is that only the front is covered.

ideas.name: Knocker-up
ideas.idea: Paid to wake workers by tapping bedroom windows with a long pole. When the Knocker-up passes within 4 m of a house window, the pole taps it: the house wakes for 10 s and the living inside pelt the street, harming all dead within 4 m of that wall each second. A house cannot be woken again for 20 s. The thumb hugs the walls and plans a round of house-fronts. Starting skill, Rap: strikes one dead between 1.5 and 4.5 m away, never nearer.
ideas.source: Knockers-up walked a round before dawn tapping clients' upper windows with a long pole and did not leave until the sleeper showed at the glass.
ideas.nearest: Characters who switch on turrets or shrines by passing them. Here the turrets are the district's own houses, so the class's power lies in a route along walls.

ideas.name: Ferryman
ideas.idea: Takes fares. One quiet dead at a time waits at a landing stair holding up a coin. Walk through it and it climbs on the Ferryman's back: 15% slower while loaded. Carry it to the opposite stair, marked by a lamp, and it steps off for good, paying experience equal to 10 kills and one coin. Below half life the fare slips off. The thumb plays there-and-back crossings through the horde. Starting skill, Sweep: every 1.5 s the oar swings a 3 m half-circle behind the direction of travel.
ideas.source: Ferrymen carried passengers between named stairs for a fixed fare, and the coins on a corpse's eyes were called the fare for the last crossing.
ideas.nearest: Delivery and escort objectives, and couriers who walk loads across hostile ground as in Death Stranding. Here it is one class's way of levelling inside a horde fight, and the passenger is one of the dead, paid off instead of killed.

ideas.name: Toll-keeper
ideas.idea: Keeps the bar at bridge and gate. One button plants the toll-post where the keeper stands. A bar then runs from post to keeper, up to 7 m long, and moves as the keeper moves. Every dead thing the bar passes over pays toll: harm equal to one blow, doubled each time the same thing pays again within 10 s. Because the dead chase the keeper, circling the post sweeps the bar through them like a clock hand. Starting skill: the bar itself.
ideas.source: A turnpike was a bar across the road beside the toll-house, swung aside for those who paid, and the charge was levied again at every passing.
ideas.nearest: Tether and beam-between-two-points weapons in arcade shooters. Here one end is fixed by the player, the charge doubles per crossing, and the play pattern is an orbit round a post.

ideas.name: Glazier
ideas.idea: Carries a leaded panel of coloured glass on a pole. Each district has one fixed great light: a rose window, a beacon, a low moon. The panel throws a coloured patch on the ground, 3 m wide, lying 2 to 5 m from the Glazier on the side away from that light. Only dead standing in the patch are harmed, 4 times a second. The thumb keeps the light at its back and the crowd down-light; where a building blocks the light, the patch fails. Starting skill: the patch.
ideas.source: Leaded glass is small coloured panes held in lead cames, and what it does is throw a patch of coloured light on the floor away from the window.
ideas.nearest: Fixed-offset damage zones and flashlight cones. Here the direction of the offset belongs to the district, not the character, so the class plays differently on every map and uses the game's real light.

ideas.name: Organ-blower
ideas.idea: Pumps the organ's bellows. Skills never cast while the Blower moves. Walking fills the wind-chest, 1 unit per metre, up to 30; a weight on a string above the figure shows how full it is. Standing still lets the wind out: all skills cast at 3 times their rate, spending 10 units a second, and stop when the chest is empty. The thumb alternates a 30 m run with a 3 s stand. Starting skill, Stop: a pipe note harming a cone 6 m long.
ideas.source: An organ made no sound unless a blower pumped its bellows by hand, and a tell-tale weight showed how much wind was left.
ideas.nearest: Charge-by-moving items and stand-to-fire characters. Here movement is the only fuel and standing the only trigger, with the gauge hung above the figure.

ideas.name: Fossor (from Sexton)
ideas.idea: Every grave the Sexton digs now throws up a spoil bank: a wall of earth 3 m long on the far side of the grave from where the Sexton walked in. The dead cannot cross a bank and are turned round its ends, toward the pit. A bank lasts until its grave is full; then the earth goes back in and both vanish. With 4 graves open the Sexton has 4 walls to place, and each stop is chosen for the pen it completes as much as for the pit.
ideas.source: Digging a grave throws up a heap of spoil beside it, which stays there until the grave is filled in.
ideas.nearest: Wall-placing abilities and tower-defence mazing. These walls come only as the by-product of the class's own traps and are removed when the traps succeed.

ideas.name: Sin-eater (from Sexton)
ideas.idea: A new rule about bodies. Standing on a fallen body for 0.5 s eats its sin: that body is laid for good whatever it was owed, and gives double experience. Each body eaten adds 1 Sin to the Sin-eater: 1% more harm dealt and 0.5% less speed, without limit. Sin is shed only by leaving through a gate, where each point becomes 1 Echo. The Sin-eater grows stronger and slower through a vigil until staying is no longer possible, and must judge which body is the last worth eating.
ideas.source: The sin-eater was paid to eat bread and drink ale over a corpse, taking its sins so that it would lie quiet, and pledged his own soul for it.
ideas.nearest: Stacking on-kill buffs. This one is taken body by body on purpose, costs speed with no ceiling, and turns into permanent currency only by leaving alive.

ideas.name: Beadle of the Procession (from Verger)
ideas.idea: Dead parted by the Verger's wedge no longer close in behind. For 5 s they fall into two files 1.5 m apart and follow the Verger's exact path at the Verger's pace, unable to strike; the files hold up to 40. If the Verger stops, or turns more than 90 degrees within a second, the files break: everyone in them strikes at once and moves 30% faster for 3 s. A surrounding crowd becomes a column, and anything that harms along a line has something to aim down.
ideas.source: The beadle marshalled the parish procession into order behind the verger and kept it in file.
ideas.nearest: Kiting a train of enemies, which happens by accident in most horde games. Here the column is a state with rules, a size, and a penalty for breaking it.

ideas.name: Curfew-warden (from Knocker-up)
ideas.idea: A house that is awake can be covered. Passing a woken house a second time while it is still awake raps it shut: its windows go dark and every dead thing within 4 m of that wall, up to 12, lies down asleep where it stands. Sleepers cannot be harmed, give nothing and block nothing. All of them wake together at the next toll. The warden uses the street to put part of the horde off until the bell, and must then be somewhere else when it rings.
ideas.source: At the curfew bell every household had to cover its fire and put out its lights for the night.
ideas.nearest: Sleep effects that break on damage. These sleepers cannot be touched at all and wake on the district's bell, so the effect is a loan against the next toll.

ideas.name: The Mute (from Knocker-up)
ideas.idea: The Knocker-up falls silent. The dead find the living by sound: any dead thing more than 6 m from the Mute no longer knows where the Mute is, and walks instead to the loudest thing it can hear, which is the nearest woken house. They crowd under the windows that are pelting them. The Mute's own Rap makes no sound. The class stops being chased and starts placing the horde, house by house; anything within 6 m still sees it and gives chase.
ideas.source: Hired mutes stood silent at the door of a house of death, and the knocker-up's whole trade was deciding who heard what.
ideas.nearest: Stealth with noise-maker decoys. Here the decoys are the houses the class already wakes, and the whole horde, not a guard or two, goes to them.

ideas.name: Dredgerman (from Ferryman)
ideas.idea: The Ferryman may now carry a body instead of a fare. Walking over the body of an elite loads it: 25% slower. Either stair will take it. The near stair, on this bank, pays a finding fee of 5 coin. The far stair, across the district, pays three times as much, 15 coin, and adds one property to the best item that body drops. While a body is carried, the dead move 10% faster, drawn to it. Every elite laid sets the same question: near bank or far.
ideas.source: Thames dredgermen were paid a reward for each drowned body they brought in, and one bank of the river paid about three times what the other did.
ideas.nearest: Carry-the-objective modes, and carrying a corpse to be disposed of in Death Stranding. The body here is a product of ordinary play, and the same delivery has a cheap near price and a dear far one.

ideas.name: Burgess of the Bar (from Toll-keeper)
ideas.idea: A dead thing that pays at the Toll-keeper's bar three times and is still standing is made quit of toll: free of the city. It stops fighting, walks to the nearest gate and leaves, and at the gate pays 3 coin into what the keeper carries. Freed dead give no experience. The bar now has two uses, and the keeper chooses by how hard it hits: strong enough to lay the crowd for experience, or light enough that the crowd survives three payings and walks out as coin.
ideas.source: A burgess who had paid his dues was quit of toll and passed every bar in the realm free.
ideas.nearest: Effects that turn kills into gold instead of experience. Here the conversion needs the enemy to survive three hits, so the player tunes a weapon to be weak on purpose.

ideas.name: Clerk of the Bills (from Toll-keeper)
ideas.idea: At each toll the Clerk publishes a Bill: a count of every kind of dead laid since the last toll. The kind with the highest count is struck from the roll: none of that kind rise during the next interval. The numbers must still be made up, so every other kind rises 15% more. The Bill is shown as it fills. By steering toward one kind and leaving another alone, the player chooses which part of the horde the district will be missing for the next 75 s.
ideas.source: Parish clerks compiled the weekly Bills of Mortality from the searchers' reports: a count of the dead under each cause.
ideas.nearest: Banishing an enemy type from the pool through a menu. Here the choice is made by what the player actually lays most, is renewed at every toll, and is paid for in more of the rest.

ideas.name: Rose-wright (from Glazier)
ideas.idea: The second button plants the Glazier's panel in the ground, where it stands until the next toll and keeps throwing its patch from the district's fixed light; a new panel is carried at once. Up to 3 stand at a time. Planted patches harm at half force, but where patches overlap their harm adds, and a patch that falls on another panel passes through it and is thrown a second time, further on. The Rose-wright builds a window across a street and fights in the pool of colour behind it.
ideas.source: A rose window is many small panels set in one frame, each throwing its own colour onto the same floor.
ideas.nearest: Placed turrets. These have no aim of their own: where they act is fixed by the map's one light, so placing them is geometry rather than coverage.

ideas.name: Sale by Candle
ideas.idea: Every 12 s an inch of candle is set down at the thickest group within 8 m and burns for 4 to 7 s. While it burns, every blow the player lands on dead within 4 m of it is a bid: its harm is also added to a pot. When the flame dies the whole pot falls on the one dead thing the player struck last. The flame flares for 0.5 s before it dies; the player uses that warning to step beside the target that ought to win.
ideas.source: In a sale by candle the last bid before the flame went out took the lot, and Pepys noted that the wick flares just before it dies.
ideas.nearest: Abilities that store damage and release it on one marked target. Here the store is filled by fighting a crowd, the winner is whoever was struck last, and the end is random with a short tell.

ideas.name: Steelyard
ideas.idea: Every 9 s the two dead nearest the player are hung on the weigh-beam for 1 s, shown as a bar joining them. The one with more remaining life loses the difference, up to 30% of its full life; the lighter one is unharmed. The skill does nothing to two fresh bodies and most when one is nearly finished and the other is a brute, so the player herds a wounded straggler alongside the thing they want cut down, and keeps both closer than anything else.
ideas.source: Market toll was charged by weight on the town's public weigh-beam, where the two sides had to be brought level.
ideas.nearest: Health-equalising spells in turn-based games. Here it is automatic, takes only the nearest pair, and the player's part is arranging who that pair is.

ideas.name: Resting Stones
ideas.idea: Every 10 s a resting stone is set where the player stands; only the newest two remain. The straight line between them is a corpse road, up to 14 m long. Dead that come within 2 m of the road are taken onto it and must walk along it to the newer stone, feet first, unable to turn or strike, then stand there 1 s before they are free. The player lays the road so that it carries the crowd away, or through ground the other skills have prepared.
ideas.source: The dead were carried to the mother church along fixed corpse roads, feet first and never turning back, the bier set down only at resting stones.
ideas.nearest: Conveyor lanes in tower defence, and skills that pull enemies to a point. Here the lane is drawn by where the player last stood twice, and it only moves bodies along it.

ideas.name: Month's Mind
ideas.idea: Every dead thing the player lays is remembered. Exactly 30 s after it fell, one bell-note sounds at the spot where it died, harming everything within 3 m for 40% of what that body's full life was. The newest 40 deaths are kept. A faint ring on the ground marks each spot and closes as its time nears. The player learns to bring the crowd back, half a minute later, across the ground where the last fight was thickest.
ideas.source: A month's mind was a mass said for a dead person one month after the death: a remembrance owed at a fixed, known time.
ideas.nearest: Delayed explosions and time bombs. These are placed by the kills themselves, come due on a fixed half-minute, and scale with what died there, which sets the player a lap time.

ideas.name: Rap at the Grave
ideas.idea: The graves from which the next toll's dead will rise are visible as mounds during the 75 s before. Every 5 s the skill raps the nearest unopened mound within 8 m. Its occupant rises at once with 40% life and stands unready for 2 s; left alone it would rise at the toll with full life and that toll's added danger. A rapped body gives full experience. The player spends the quiet seconds touring the mounds to thin the wave before the bell brings it.
ideas.source: The knocker-up's trade was waking sleepers before the bell did, at an hour chosen in advance.
ideas.nearest: Calling the next wave early for a bonus in tower defence. Here it is done body by body, by walking to each grave, and what comes up early comes up weak.

ideas.name: Split Tally
ideas.idea: Every 6 s the skill cuts a tally against the 8 dead nearest the player; each carries its half, shown as a pale stick on its chest, for 10 s. Every point of harm the player deals to such a body is also notched on the stick. When the player passes within 1.5 m of it, the two halves are fitted and the whole notched sum is dealt again at once. A half nobody fits lapses unpaid. Wound from far off, then brush past.
ideas.source: A debt was notched on a stick that was then split lengthwise; creditor and debtor each kept half, and the debt was proved when the halves were fitted together.
ideas.nearest: Mark-and-detonate skills. Here the trigger is physical nearness, so collecting is a risk taken with the thumb, and the amount is exactly what was notched.

ideas.name: Tellers
ideas.idea: Every 6 s the hand-bell tells the nearest dead thing within 8 m: three strokes if it is small, six if middling, nine if large, a quarter-second apart. Each stroke harms it and everything within 2 m of it. If it falls before its count is finished, the strokes left over are told on its nearest neighbour and count double. The player gets most from it by standing nearest to something large that is already close to falling, in the middle of a crowd.
ideas.source: The death knell began with tellers, three times three strokes for a man, three times two for a woman, three for a child, so that hearers could count who had died.
ideas.nearest: Burst attacks that move to a new target when the first dies. Here the length of the burst is read off the size of the victim, and unspent strokes pass on at double weight.

ideas.name: Lamp and Long Shadow
ideas.idea: Every 8 s the skill lights the nearest street-lamp within 8 m for 12 s. A lit lamp makes every dead thing within 9 m of it throw a real cast shadow on the ground, pointing away from the lamp and as long as the thing's distance from it. For the player's skills that shadow counts as part of the body: whatever strikes the shadow strikes its owner. The player fights with a lamp between themselves and the crowd, so the shadows reach toward them.
ideas.source: Lamplighters walked a fixed round lighting each street-lamp with a long pole, and a low lamp makes every figure throw a long shadow behind it.
ideas.nearest: Folk tales of pinning someone by their shadow, and enlarged hit areas on marked enemies. Here the enlargement is the visible shadow drawn by the game's real light, so its direction and length are read straight off the screen.

ideas.name: Founder's Pit
ideas.idea: Every 20 s a casting pit 2 m across is dug where the player stands and stays open 12 s. Each dead thing that falls within 5 m of it pours into the mould, so the player must hold that ground. When the 12 s are up the bell is struck once. With 8 or more poured it rings: harm to everything within 2 m plus 0.3 m per body, equal to a quarter of the summed full life of the bodies poured. With fewer it cracks and does nothing.
ideas.source: Great bells were cast in a pit dug beside the tower they were meant for, and a short pour made a cracked bell fit only to be broken up.
ideas.nearest: Totems charged by nearby kills. This one is all or nothing at a known count, and its size is the bodies themselves.

ideas.name: Ledger Stones
ideas.idea: Every 4 s a ledger stone, 2 m by 1 m, is laid flat on the spot where the last dead thing fell, and stays for the whole vigil, up to 60 stones. The dead walk 25% slower on a ledger; the player walks 15% faster. Where 6 or more stones touch they make a floor: nothing can rise up through a floor, and a body that falls on one never stands again. The player paves a home ground by choosing where the killing is done.
ideas.source: Ledger stones are the inscribed slabs a mason sets flat in a church floor over graves, until the whole floor is paved with them.
ideas.nearest: Slowing ground effects. These are permanent, are placed by where kills happen, and join into a floor that denies rising, so the player is building territory.

ideas.name: Hatchment
ideas.idea: Every 14 s a lozenge 7 m across is laid on the ground at the player's feet for 8 s, split down its length into a black half and a white half. Dead standing on black take 50% more harm; dead standing on white deal 50% less. The same binds the player: on black the player takes 50% more, on white deals 50% less. The split runs along the direction the player was walking when it was laid, so the thumb sets the board and then picks a side.
ideas.source: A hatchment showed the dead person's arms on a lozenge whose ground was black behind the dead spouse's half and white behind the survivor's.
ideas.nearest: Buff and debuff zones. This is one zone with two opposite halves whose rule binds the player as well, so the question is always who is standing where.

ideas.name: Dexter and Sinister
ideas.idea: The skill is split down the line the player is walking. Whatever it strikes on the player's right hand (dexter) takes 70% more harm; whatever it strikes on the left (sinister) takes 70% less. The split turns with the thumb, lagging 0.3 s, and holds its last line when the player stands still. Cost: half the skill's field is nearly dead, so the player must keep steering to put the crowd on the right, and a skill that only acts straight ahead gains nothing.
ideas.source: On a hatchment the dexter half stood for the husband and the sinister for the wife, and the black half showed which of them was dead.
ideas.nearest: Backstab and flank bonuses tied to the enemy's facing. This is tied to the player's own heading and to left and right, which I have not seen used.

ideas.name: Easting
ideas.idea: Blows from this skill that travel westward, pushing the dead back down onto their backs, deal double harm; blows that travel eastward deal half; north and south are unchanged, with a smooth scale between. Against risen clergy, who were buried the other way round, the rule is reversed. Cost: the skill is worth having only while the player keeps to the east of what it is aimed at. Every district's compass is fixed and can be read from which way its gravestones face.
ideas.source: Christians were buried with feet to the east so as to rise facing east, and by custom priests were laid the opposite way, to rise facing their flock.
ideas.nearest: none known; directional bonuses in games are relative to the target's facing, not to the compass of the map.

ideas.name: Foil
ideas.idea: The skill keeps only half its harm, the stock. The other half is left on the target as a foil, shown as a notch, for 8 s. When a different skill of the same character next strikes that target, the halves fit: the foil is paid at double, so the pair together deal 150% of the first skill's harm. Striking again with the same skill only renews the foil. Cost: alone the skill does half its harm; it needs a partner skill that reaches the same bodies within 8 s.
ideas.source: One half of a split tally was worth nothing by itself; stock and foil proved the debt only when the two were fitted.
ideas.nearest: Supports that reward alternating two damage types. This pairs two particular skills on the same body, and a half that is never fitted is simply lost.

ideas.name: Lych-wait
ideas.idea: The skill no longer casts the moment it is ready. It waits, as the bier waits under the lychgate for the priest, until at least 5 dead stand inside the place it would strike, or until 4 s have passed. For every full second it waited, its harm rises 20%. Cost: against a thin or scattered crowd the skill casts late and seldom. The player makes it work by drawing the dead into a knot and holding them there until it lets go.
ideas.source: At the lychgate the bearers set the bier down under the roof and waited for the priest to come out and meet it before going further.
ideas.nearest: Charge-up supports. Here the skill decides for itself when the shot is worth taking, by a rule the player can see and feed.

ideas.name: Passes Free
ideas.idea: The first dead thing the skill would strike is let through untouched. The skill passes on and strikes the next thing along its path, or the next nearest to its centre, and that blow deals 60% more. If there is no second target the cast is wasted. Cost: the skill can never harm the thing nearest the player, so it must be paired with something that can. It is for reaching the keeper standing behind its crowd.
ideas.source: Some travellers passed the toll-bar free: funerals, the mail, and burgesses whose town was quit of toll.
ideas.nearest: Piercing shots that carry on after the first hit. This one skips the first body entirely, which reverses what the skill is good against.

ideas.name: Narrowing Border
ideas.idea: At each toll the skill's area starts 80% wider than normal and its harm 40% lower. With every cast after that, the area shrinks by a tenth of normal and the harm rises by a tenth, until the area is at 50% and the harm at 190%; the next toll sets it wide again. Cost: the skill is never one thing for long: wide and weak when the toll's crowd arrives, narrow and heavy once only its strong ones are left.
ideas.source: Mourning stationery carried a black border that was made narrower at each stage of the mourning term.
ideas.nearest: Ramping buffs that reset on a timer. Here size is traded for weight step by step, and the reset is the district bell.

ideas.name: Indenture
ideas.idea: The cast is cut in two along a wavy line. The halves leave the player 40 degrees apart, curve, and meet again at exactly 7 m. Along their separate paths each half deals 50% of the skill's harm; at the meeting point, where the cut edges fit, they deal 300% in a circle 1.5 m across. Cost: the skill is weak at every distance but one, so the thumb must hold its target 7 m off, neither nearer nor farther.
ideas.source: An indenture was written out twice on one sheet and cut apart along a wavy line, so that the two copies proved each other when the edges were matched.
ideas.nearest: Sweet-spot weapons that hit harder at the tip. This one has two weak travelling halves and a single point where they are worth six times as much.

ideas.name: The Vigil Candle
ideas.idea: The pool that vows hold is the character's vigil candle, 12 inches long. One inch burns away at every toll. A vow does not use candle up; it holds inches back unburnt: with a 3-inch vow kept, only 9 inches are left to burn. When no free candle remains, every vow goes dark until wax is found (a keeper drops 3 inches). So a vow is paid for in time: three vows give a strong first six tolls and nothing after, one vow lasts the night.
ideas.source: A wake was timed by its candles, and an endowment held capital back untouched so that it could go on paying.
ideas.nearest: Reserving a share of a resource bar for lasting effects. Here the bar is also the run's clock, so the price of each vow is how long any vow lasts.

ideas.name: Full Mourning
ideas.idea: Holds 4 inches of the pool. The character wears full black, and the dead cannot make the wearer out beyond 7 m: those farther off lose them and walk to where they last saw them. But nothing bright may be taken in full mourning: coin and gear are not picked up, only experience. At every third toll the mourning lightens a grade: grey, seen at 10 m, coin allowed; then lavender, seen at 14 m. To return to black the vow must be dropped and taken again at a gate.
ideas.source: Full mourning forbade anything shiny, even jewellery other than jet, and lightened by set stages to grey and then lavender.
ideas.nearest: Stealth effects that shorten enemy sight. This one forbids loot while it holds and wears off in grades timed by the bell.

ideas.name: Tell the Bees
ideas.idea: Holds 3 inches of the pool. A hive rides on the character's back and its bees fetch every pickup within 10 m. In return the bees must be told of every important death: within 10 s of an elite or keeper falling anywhere in the district, the player must stand still for 1 s. If a death goes untold the bees leave until the next toll, taking what they were carrying. Each telling also sends the bees to drive the 5 nearest dead back 3 m.
ideas.source: Bees had to be told of a death in the household, with a knock on the hive, or they would leave or stop making honey.
ideas.nearest: Pickup-magnet companions. This one carries a duty that makes the player stand still for a second at the worst moment, just after a big kill.

ideas.name: Deodand
ideas.idea: Holds 3 inches. Once every 10 s, the next thing that harms the character is declared deodand. If it was moving when it struck, it changes sides for 6 s; if it was standing, it cannot strike for 6 s; a ground patch goes dark for 6 s. The holder is paid its appraised value: coin equal to 5% of that thing's full life. Since the first harm in each 10 s is the one seized, the player can pick it, and walk into a charger on purpose.
ideas.source: The coroner's jury named the object that had caused a death, appraised it, and declared it forfeit as a deodand.
ideas.nearest: Thorns and reflect effects. This seizes the attacker instead of hurting it, pays by what the attacker was worth, and rewards choosing which blow to take.

ideas.name: Ring Your Own Knell
ideas.idea: The character's passing bell is rung and the dead take them for one of their own. Until the next toll nothing new rises, and the dead already standing ignore the character unless struck. But everything that should have risen in that time is only held back, and all of it rises together at the toll, on top of the toll's own wave. Taken when the player needs up to 75 quiet seconds to collect, cross the district or reach a gate, and can afford what follows.
ideas.source: The passing bell was rung for a person who was dying but not yet dead, so the parish heard of the death before it happened.
ideas.nearest: Invisibility and wave-skip pickups. Nothing is skipped here: it is postponed and delivered in one piece on the bell.

ideas.name: Funeral Biscuit
ideas.idea: A biscuit wrapped in printed paper and sealed with black wax. Sealed, it does nothing. At any later level-up the player may break the seal instead of choosing: it then counts as two picks, both taken from that level-up's offers. If it is still sealed when the character leaves through a gate, it is kept as a token and adds 20% to the Echoes that vigil leaves. If the character dies with it sealed, the player's next character starts its first vigil holding it.
ideas.source: Funeral guests were given biscuits wrapped in printed paper and sealed with black wax, often kept for years as a remembrance or sent to those who could not come.
ideas.nearest: Banked rerolls and saved level-ups. This has three different ends, depending on whether it is opened, carried out, or left behind by the dead.

ideas.name: Coins on Your Own Eyes
ideas.idea: The ferryman is paid in advance. From now on a gate opens for this character at every toll, 20 m from where they stand, for 15 s, instead of only from time to time. The fare is 2 coins out of what the character carries, taken at each toll whether the gate is used or not, and it rises by 1 each toll. The first time the fare cannot be paid the pick is lost, and no gate at all opens for the next two tolls.
ideas.source: The coins laid on a dead person's eyes were said to be the fare owed to the ferryman for the last crossing.
ideas.nearest: Extraction beacons bought in extraction games. This is a standing subscription to exits, paid from the same purse the exits exist to save.

ideas.name: Short Tally
ideas.idea: Take any one of the other picks on offer at double effect, but as a tally: the character holds the stock and the gate holds the foil. The tally must be fitted by leaving through a gate within three tolls. If the third toll passes and the character is still in the district, the tally is void: the doubled pick is removed, and so is the pick taken before it. A way to burn bright for under four minutes and then go.
ideas.source: A tally bound both parties to a day of reckoning; after that day an unmatched half was a stick of firewood.
ideas.nearest: Timed power-ups. This one is ended by the player choosing to leave, and overstaying costs an extra pick.

ideas.name: The Weigh-in
ideas.idea: At the next toll, the coin the character is carrying is weighed on the town beam. For every 20 coins on them at that moment they deal 2% more harm for the rest of the vigil. Until that toll the pick gives nothing, and after it carrying coin gives no more. Coin carried is coin not yet banked, and falls with the character. So the player must stay away from gates, and alive, for at most 75 s with as full a purse as they dare.
ideas.source: Market toll was reckoned on the public weigh-beam at the moment the goods crossed it, neither before nor after.
ideas.nearest: Damage-per-gold items. This is measured once, at a known moment, so it asks for one risky minute rather than permanent hoarding.

ideas.name: Pall on Hire
ideas.idea: The parish pall is hired for a term of two tolls. While it covers the character, the first blow in every 3 s is turned aside. When the term ends the pall must be returned in person: a chest appears at the far side of the district, and the player has one toll to walk into it. Returned in time, the hire cost nothing and the pall may be offered again later. Not returned, the deposit is taken: the next two level-ups offer no pick.
ideas.source: Parishes owned a pall and hired it out for each funeral, to be brought back afterwards.
ideas.nearest: Temporary shields. This one is rented, and giving it back is an errand across the map with a penalty counted in future picks.

ideas.name: Make Your Will
ideas.idea: Name one of the character's skills in a will. Nothing changes now. If this character dies in this vigil, that skill passes whole, with its bindings exactly as they stood, to another of the player's characters, chosen afterwards. If the character leaves the vigil alive the will is torn up, and in exchange its next vigil's first level-up offers one extra pick. A pick that is worth most to a character the player expects to lose.
ideas.source: Mourning rings and named goods were left by will to chosen people, and changed hands only on the death.
ideas.nearest: Insurance slots in extraction games. This insures a built skill rather than loot, and pays a small refund if it is never needed.

ideas.name: The Coin-Eyed
ideas.idea: Properly buried, coins still on its eyes, so it cannot see. It walks in a dead straight line until it bumps a wall or a body, then turns to face the last loud sound, the player's most recent cast, and sets off straight again. It harms by walking into things, the other dead included. Read it by two bright discs on its face and a ruler-straight path. Step aside; it drops its two coins when laid, so a line of them is worth leading into a wall.
ideas.source: Coins were laid on the eyes of the dead to keep them shut and to pay the ferryman.
ideas.nearest: Blind enemies that hunt by sound in stealth games. Here blindness makes a straight-line walker inside a homing horde, and the coins are its loot.

ideas.name: The Mute
ideas.idea: A hired mourner still at its post. It never moves: it stands in a doorway, gate or lane-mouth holding a tall wand draped in cloth, and does no harm. But within 5 m of it nothing makes a sound, so the player's skills do not cast there. Read it by the tall black pole and its perfect stillness. The cure is to walk up and jostle it: a touch knocks the wand down for 6 s, and in that time it falls to two blows.
ideas.source: Hired mutes stood silent at the door of a house of death holding wands draped in black crape.
ideas.nearest: Silence fields cast by enemy spellcasters. This one is a harmless standing figure that guards exits, and the answer is to go and bump into it.

ideas.name: The Bier Party
ideas.idea: Four dead bearers carry a fifth on a bier along the district's corpse road toward the bell. They ignore the player, never leave the road, and pause 3 s at each resting stone to set the bier down. If the bier reaches the lychgate the body is received and rises as an elite at the next toll. Lay the bearers on the move and the bier is dropped: the body wakes at once. Lay them while the bier rests on a stone and it sleeps on, and can be searched.
ideas.source: Bearers carried the bier along the corpse road and might set it down only at the resting stones.
ideas.nearest: Caravans and escorts to be intercepted. Here where the player strikes matters more than whether, and the map marks the right places in advance.

ideas.name: The Mortsafe
ideas.idea: Risen with its iron cage still locked on. Caged, it shuffles toward the player and can neither strike nor be harmed. The lock has a term of 6 s, shown as six bars that vanish one by one, and every blow on the cage puts one bar back. When the last bar goes it bursts out, three times as fast and striking hard, but with little life. Skills that keep hitting it keep it harmless and waste their blows; the player must walk away, let it open, and meet it.
ideas.source: A mortsafe was an iron cage locked over a new grave for a term of weeks, then taken off once the body was past use to the anatomists.
ideas.nearest: Shielded enemies with a break window. Here hitting the shield renews it, so the answer is to stop attacking, which self-casting skills make hard.

ideas.name: The Searcher
ideas.idea: An old woman with a white wand, risen to finish her round. She keeps 7 m from the player and levels the wand, drawn as a white line. If the line rests unbroken on the player for 3 s she reports the cause: for 15 s every dead thing in the district deals 50% more harm to that character. The line is broken by any body standing in it, so the player hides behind the horde itself. She has little life but backs away from whoever comes at her.
ideas.source: Searchers of the dead were old women who examined each body, carried a white wand so that people could keep clear of them, and reported the cause to the parish clerk.
ideas.nearest: Snipers with a visible aiming line. This one emboldens the others instead of shooting, and the cover the player uses is the enemy crowd.

ideas.name: The Link-boy
ideas.idea: A dead child with a torch, a real light. It does not chase: it runs 4 m ahead of the player in whatever direction the player is heading, and never strikes. Dead standing in its torchlight can see their way and move 40% faster. It is always lighting the ground the player is about to run onto. Read it by the small figure and the bright pool ahead. A sharp turn leaves it behind for 2 s; one blow lays it, but only skills that reach forward can catch it.
ideas.source: Link-boys carried torches ahead of people walking at night for a farthing, and some led their customers to waiting robbers.
ideas.nearest: Support enemies that carry a buff zone. This one takes its position from the player's own heading, so it punishes running in a straight line.

ideas.name: Dole-seekers
ideas.idea: The parish poor, risen for the funeral dole. They come as a slow crowd of 20 with open hands, never strike, and fall to one blow. Each takes the first experience pickup it reaches, then turns and leaves the district, saying the prayer it owes: the player gains one ward-stroke, which stops one blow, 20 at most. They turn experience into protection one for one. Laying one gives nothing and makes the others take two pickups each. Read them by pale colour and flat upturned hands.
ideas.source: The poor came to funerals for the dole of bread or pence, and owed a prayer for the dead in return.
ideas.nearest: Thief enemies that grab pickups and run. These pay for what they take, and the choice is whether to let them.

ideas.name: The Forfeit Wheel
ideas.idea: A forfeit thing, not a body: the cartwheel, millstone or fallen clapper that once killed someone. It rolls in straight lines at twice walking pace, bouncing off walls and harming whatever it runs over, dead or living. It cannot be destroyed. Its next two bounces are drawn on the ground. If it strikes the player it is forfeit again, this time to them: for 15 s it bends its path toward the nearest dead after every bounce, then stops for good. Being hit once is how to own it.
ideas.source: A deodand was the object that had caused a death, such as a cartwheel, forfeit because it had moved to the death.
ideas.nearest: Indestructible bouncing hazards in arcade games. This one changes owner when it hurts the player, so taking the hit is a tactic.

ideas.name: Resurrection-men
ideas.idea: Living thieves, in pairs, with sack and spade. They run against the flow of the horde to wherever bodies and pickups lie thickest, stuff up to 6 into the sack in 3 s, and make for the district's edge. They never strike, and the dead ignore them. Two blows drop one and spill the sack. They are also a free way to be rid of bodies that would stand again at the toll, so sometimes the player lets them work and guards only the coin.
ideas.source: Body-snatchers dug up the newly buried by night to sell to anatomists, which is why graves were caged and watched.
ideas.nearest: Loot goblins and pickup thieves. These take the player's uncollected leavings, and because they also remove bodies they are sometimes welcome.

ideas.name: The Layer
ideas.idea: Sixteen dead from a plague pit, risen as they were laid: one flat rank four by four, white with lime, locked shoulder to shoulder. The layer moves as a single slab 4 m square, slowly, and turns no faster than 30 degrees a second. Nothing can push through it or part it, and it harms along its whole leading edge. Its members fall one by one, leaving gaps; when 8 are gone it breaks up into ordinary dead. Get round to its side, where it cannot turn in time.
ideas.source: Plague dead were tipped into pits in layers and covered with lime, without coffins or separate graves.
ideas.nearest: Shield-wall formations in strategy games. In a horde game this is one rigid slab that the player out-turns rather than outruns.

ideas.name: Keeper of the Passing Bell
ideas.idea: Phase one, the tellers: three sets of three strokes, each a ring spreading from him to 12 m in 1.5 s with one 60-degree gap, the gap shown 1 s ahead as a pale wedge. Phase two, below 60% life, the age: one stroke for every level the character has, each a 2 m circle drawn under the player 0.8 s before it lands. Phase three, below 25%: he digs graves, outlined 1.2 s before they open; he is laid only by leading him across one of his own.
ideas.source: The death knell told the sex of the dead by sets of three strokes and then the age, one stroke for each year.
ideas.nearest: Ring-with-a-gap boss patterns are common. The barrage whose length is the player's own level, and a keeper finished by his own graves, are the parts I have not seen.

ideas.name: Keeper of the Chantry Bell
ideas.idea: He has no life, only an endowment: a chest of 600 coin beside him. Every attack is a mass that must be paid for. Phase one, trentals: lines of sound shown 0.7 s ahead, 5 coin each. Phase two, below 400, obits: a 9 m circle shown 2.5 s ahead, 60 coin. Phase three, below 150, he begs: quick cheap strokes, 2 coin each. He falls when the chest is empty. The player baits costly attacks, or robs the chest: stand on it 2 s to take 30 coin, kept.
ideas.source: A chantry was an endowment that paid a priest to sing masses for one soul for exactly as long as the money lasted.
ideas.nearest: Survive-the-timer bosses and bosses that tire. Here the timer is a visible purse that the boss spends by attacking and the player can rob.

ideas.name: Keeper of the Pest Bell
ideas.idea: Phase one, the search: a white line follows the player; where it rests 2 s, thickening, the searcher-general names the character's most-used skill and seals it for 10 s. Phase two, below 65% life, the Bill: the three kinds of dead this character has laid most in this vigil rise again, 30 bodies in the same proportions, from mounds shown 2 s ahead. Phase three, below 30%: the house is shut. Four walls, outlined 2 s ahead, close a 10 m square round her and the player for 20 s.
ideas.source: Searchers reported each death's cause for the weekly Bills of Mortality, and a plague house was shut up for a term with its people inside.
ideas.nearest: Bosses that summon helpers. The helpers here are a replay of the player's own kill count, so the fight differs with how the vigil was played.

ideas.name: Keeper of the Sanctuary Bell
ideas.idea: The floor is lit by a hearse of 15 candles. In each of three rounds, every pattern the keeper finishes (lines of sound, shown 1 s ahead) puts one candle out, and the lit ground shrinks; the player's skills pick only targets standing in light. The last candle is carried behind the altar: 4 s of dark, in which a faint glow marks the one safe spot, then the crash, harming everything elsewhere. The candle returns, all 15 relight, and the keeper kneels open to harm for 6 s.
ideas.source: At Tenebrae fifteen candles on a triangular hearse were put out one by one, the last was hidden, a crash was made in the dark, and the candle was brought back.
ideas.nearest: Shrinking-arena and find-the-safe-spot boss phases. The device here is the game's real lighting, counted down as candles in a fixed liturgical order.

ideas.name: The Lychway
ideas.idea: One pale corpse road 6 m wide crosses the district from the far gate to the lychgate under the bell, past five resting stones. The dead rise at the far end and walk the road like a current; they leave it only for a living person within 8 m, and cannot turn back along it. The player fights from the banks, darting in. Shapes: flat slab road, low box stones, a gate of two posts and a tapered roof, cone yews. Colours: yew green, wet slate, bone, tallow yellow, rust.
ideas.source: Outlying hamlets carried their dead to the mother church along one fixed corpse road, with resting stones on the way and a lychgate at the end.
ideas.nearest: Lane maps in tower defence. In a horde-survival game, a horde with a known course that is fought from the side is unusual.

ideas.name: The Shut Parish
ideas.idea: No dead come in from the edges. Every house door bears a red cross with a term: the cross fades until the door opens and 5 to 12 dead come out. Standing 2 s at a door nails it shut for one more toll, but twice as many then come out. A dead-cart circles a fixed route taking every body and pickup within 2 m. Shapes: box houses, crosses of two thin boxes, a cart of one box and two cylinders. Colours: lime white, ox-blood, tar, straw, pewter.
ideas.source: A plague house was shut up for a set term with a red cross on the door, and the dead-cart made its round for the bodies.
ideas.nearest: Spawner doors in arcade shooters. Here every door shows its timer and can be put off at a price.

ideas.name: The Close
ideas.idea: Three rings lie round the cathedral door, marked by crosses at 30 m, 15 m and 4 m. The dead deal 20% less harm in the outer ring, 40% less in the middle, 70% less at the door. But sanctuary is granted for a term: each character has 40 s of each ring per vigil, counted while standing in it. A spent ring is ordinary ground. Shapes: flagstone slabs, crosses of two boxes on steps, a west front of tapered boxes. Colours: limestone, lead grey, verdigris, candle gold, window blue.
ideas.source: Beverley's sanctuary lay in rings marked by crosses, the penalty for seizing a fugitive rising toward the centre, and sanctuary lasted a fixed number of days.
ideas.nearest: Safe zones and defensive ground. These are graded, and each is a personal ration of seconds that the player spends across the vigil.

ideas.name: The Tron
ideas.idea: A market square of 30 stalls round a weigh-beam. Nothing may be sold before the bell: for 15 s after every toll the stalls open, and walking into one buys what it shows for carried coin, with no pause. The same toll raises the danger, so every bell is a dash to a stall. A stall the dead are pushed into overturns and is shut for the vigil. Shapes: box stalls with tapered striped awnings, a post-and-beam scale, a stepped cross. Colours: awning red, cream, cobble grey, brass, wet wood.
ideas.source: Markets opened on the market bell, and dealing before it rang was punished as forestalling.
ideas.nearest: Mid-run shops. These are physical, open only in the dangerous seconds after each bell, and can be destroyed by the fight.

ideas.name: Beating the Bounds
ideas.idea: The tree is drawn as a map of parishes. Points are not spent on the nodes inside a parish but on the boundary marks round it, 5 to 8 to a parish. When every mark of a parish has been taken, all the nodes inside are granted at once. Neighbouring parishes share the marks on their common border, so one point can count toward two or three parishes. Planning is choosing a block of parishes with the most shared border, and deciding which unfinished boundary is worth closing next.
ideas.source: A parish was defined by walking its boundary each year and striking every mark, and neighbouring parishes shared the marks between them.
ideas.nearest: Dots and Boxes on paper, and bonuses for filling a cluster of nodes. As the whole shape of a passive tree, paying for edges and being given areas is new to me.

ideas.name: Lapsing Tolls
ideas.idea: The tree's regions are divided by the river and the walls, and every bridge and gate between regions charges a toll of 1 to 4 extra points to cross. Each class is quit of toll at the gates of its home region. Every toll was granted for a term: printed on each crossing is the character level at which it lapses and becomes free. A planner chooses between paying 3 points to cross at level 12 and working round the home region until the bridge falls free at level 25.
ideas.source: Pontage and murage were tolls granted for a fixed term of years to repair a bridge or a wall, and certain burgesses were quit of them.
ideas.nearest: Travel nodes that cost a point and give little. Here the cost sits on the crossing itself, differs by class, and expires at a known level.

ideas.name: The Ossuary Rule
ideas.idea: Each road of the tree has room for six fresh graves. The six nodes most recently taken on a road work in full. When a seventh is taken, the oldest is lifted to the ossuary: it stays owned and keeps the path joined, but gives half. A deep road has six full nodes at its tip and a tail of halved ones, while five short roads have everything in full. The planner weighs depth against breadth, and the order of taking matters because order decides what is lifted.
ideas.source: Graves were reused after a term: the old bones were lifted and stacked in the ossuary to make room for the new dead.
ideas.nearest: Diminishing returns on stacking one stat. This works by age along a path, is visible node by node, and makes the order of purchase matter.

ideas.name: Masons' Marks
ideas.idea: Every character cuts its mark on each node it takes, and the marks stay on the shared tree after that character dies. A node bearing the marks of 3 dead characters is worn: it costs nothing to the next character who reaches it, though it must still be reached. Marks of the living do not count. Over many lives the roads the player's dead walked most become free ground, and each new character can spend its points further out than the last.
ideas.source: Each mason cut his personal mark on every stone he dressed so that his work could be counted and paid for.
ideas.nearest: Permanent unlocks bought with a meta-currency. Nothing is bought here: the discount is laid down by where dead characters actually spent their points.

ideas.name: Split Nodes
ideas.idea: Forty nodes on the tree are half-tallies. Each stock has one foil somewhere far off, usually in another class's region, with the same pattern of notches drawn on both. A half alone gives a small effect. A character holding both halves fits the tally and gains a large named effect that neither half reveals beforehand. The tree draws a thin line between the halves of every tally the player has fitted on any character, living or dead, so knowledge of the pairs is inherited.
ideas.source: The two halves of a split tally were kept by different parties and proved their bargain only when brought together.
ideas.nearest: Set bonuses, and keystones with two distant requirements. These are pairs hidden in the tree, found by matching notch patterns, and the discovery outlives the character.

ideas.name: Bequests
ideas.idea: Every item is something left by will. It carries 2 to 5 legacies, each a rolled property with a named heir: 'to my sexton', 'to one who keeps two vows'. A legacy works only while its wearer answers the description. There are no tiers: an item is as good as the fit between its heirs and its wearer. To change one, contest the will before the scrivener: strike the heir out of one legacy so that it works for anyone, and one other legacy, of the scrivener's choosing, is voided.
ideas.source: Goods and mourning rings passed by will to named persons, and contesting a will could win one claimant a legacy at another's cost.
ideas.nearest: Conditional affixes and class-restricted items. Here every property has its own condition, and crafting trades the number of properties for their freedom, one legacy at a time.

ideas.name: Halves
ideas.idea: Items drop as halves. A half is a notched stick: each notch is one property and its width is its size. A half can be worn alone at face value. Two halves whose notches fall in the same places (the same properties in the same order, at any widths) can be fitted into one whole item, with the widths added and one new notch cut where they join. To change a half, have one notch recut wider; each recut shortens the stick, and a stick has three recuts in it.
ideas.source: Exchequer tallies recorded sums as notches of set widths, and a stock fitted only its own foil.
ideas.nearest: Fusing duplicate items, and two-piece sets. This is a search for a matching pattern rather than a matching name, with a hard limit on rework.

ideas.name: Appraisal
ideas.idea: An item is found blank, with four empty lines. The first four different kinds of elite it helps to lay each write one line: a property drawn at random from that kind's own short list (a Mute's is about silence, a Bier Party's about roads) with a rolled size. The player shapes an item by choosing what it is used on first. To change it, forfeit a line to the Crown: the line is struck out, a little coin is paid, and the space waits for the next new kind.
ideas.source: A coroner's jury appraised the thing that had caused a death, and it was the death that gave the object its standing in law.
ideas.nearest: Weapons that earn traits from tracked kills. Here the kills decide which pool each random property is drawn from, in the order they happen.

ideas.name: Terms of Mourning
ideas.idea: Every item is found in full mourning, with one property showing and three veiled. Wearing it advances its term, counted in tolls stood while it is worn. At 8 tolls it lightens to grey and the second property shows; at 24, lavender and the third; at 60 it is out of mourning and the fourth shows at 150% of its roll. To change an item, send it to the dyer: it goes back to black, every property not yet shown is rolled afresh, and the count starts again.
ideas.source: Mourning was worn for fixed terms and lightened by stages, and cloth was sent back to the dyer to be made black again.
ideas.nearest: Unidentified items, and gear that levels with use. This reveals itself by time worn at risk, and a reroll costs the time already put in.

ideas.name: Bier-right
ideas.idea: A murdered body lies on a bier in the open. Three elite dead, the suspects, arrive and hunt the player. Custom says a corpse bleeds when its murderer comes near: each time a suspect passes within 2 m of the bier, the bier either stays pale or runs red. Lead them past it one at a time to find the guilty one. Lay the guilty one first and the body gives up an item with an extra property; lay an innocent first and the body rises as a fourth elite.
ideas.source: By bier-right, suspects were made to approach or touch the corpse, which was believed to bleed afresh at its murderer.
ideas.nearest: Pick-the-right-target puzzles. The test here is carried out by steering hostile elites past a spot on the ground in the middle of the fight.

ideas.name: Sanctuary
ideas.idea: Each district's church door has a knocker. Once per vigil the player may grasp it by standing at it 1 s. For a term of 40 s no dead thing may touch the character, the character's skills fall silent, and the whole build is open to change: bindings moved, points spent, vows swapped. The bell does not wait: every dead thing that arrives stands in a ring 3 m off. When the term ends, or the player lets go, the character must break out through whatever has gathered.
ideas.source: A fugitive who grasped the sanctuary knocker could not be seized for a set number of days, while his pursuers kept watch outside.
ideas.nearest: Safe rooms and rest points. This one is taken in the middle of the fight, runs on a clock, and collects a siege round itself as its price.

ideas.name: The Candle Lot
ideas.idea: A lot is set on a block in the open: one item, shown. Beside it an inch of candle burns for an unknown time between 15 and 30 s, flaring for its last second. When the flame dies, the lot goes to whoever is standing on the block, living or dead. If that is the player, the item is theirs. If it is one of the dead, that body puts the item on and becomes an elite with its properties; lay it to take the item back.
ideas.source: At a sale by candle the lot fell to the last bidder standing when the flame went out, and nobody knew when that would be.
ideas.nearest: King-of-the-hill and capture points. Here only the unknown final instant counts, and losing creates an enemy that wears the prize.

ideas.name: Hue and Cry
ideas.idea: A living body-snatcher breaks cover with a sack and runs for the far edge of the district, 60 m away. The cry goes up, and all who hear must join: for as long as he runs, every dead thing within 20 m of him chases him instead of the player. If the dead catch him, the stolen body in the sack wakes among them as an elite. If the player touches him first he drops the sack (an item and 10 coin), the cry ends, and the horde turns back.
ideas.source: Raising the hue and cry obliged everyone within hearing to leave what they were doing and pursue the felon.
ideas.nearest: Chase-the-loot-carrier events. In this one the horde is chasing him too, so it is a race against the enemies and a rest from them at once.

ideas.name: Rogation
ideas.idea: Seven bound-stones stand round the district's edge, where the dead come in. Passing within 2 m of a stone strikes it with the willow wand and it is remembered, lit, for two tolls. For each remembered stone the player's skills reach 4% further. If all seven are lit at once the bounds are beaten: until the next toll nothing rises inside them, and the district's danger steps back one toll. The circuit is some 300 m of the most dangerous ground on the map, so it is a plan.
ideas.source: Each year the parish walked its boundary and struck every mark with willow wands so that the bounds would be remembered.
ideas.nearest: Shrine and beacon circuits. This one is laid along the edge the enemies enter by, fades stone by stone, and pays in full only while the whole ring is held together.

ideas.name: The Pavement
ideas.idea: The permanent tree is not designed in advance: it is a church floor that the player paves. Every character that dies becomes one ledger stone, laid by the player on any free square beside an existing stone. Its inscription is its effect, drawn from that life: class decides the kind of effect, the district of death its condition, the toll reached its size. Echoes do not buy nodes; they cut an inscription deeper, up to three times. A stone gains 10% for each neighbouring stone of a different class.
ideas.source: Ledger stones were laid in the church floor over the dead, one by one, until the floor was made of them.
ideas.nearest: Family trees and graveyards of past characters, which are usually decoration. Here each death is a placed, upgradable node, and the layout is the player's own.

ideas.name: Hung in the Hall
ideas.idea: Whatever kills a character is forfeit to the household. The kind of dead, or the keeper, that dealt the last blow is hung in the hall as a deodand, appraised at the dead character's level. Every later character deals 1% more harm to that kind per 5 levels of appraisal and sees its attacks marked 0.2 s sooner. A kind is replaced only by a higher appraisal. Echoes are paid on top, 10 for each level appraised. Dying to something new is the richest way to lose a character.
ideas.source: The thing that had caused a death was appraised by the coroner's jury and forfeited, its value put to pious use.
ideas.nearest: Bestiary bonuses earned by kills, and nemesis systems that promote whoever killed you. Here the reward comes from being killed, once per kind, and is sized by what was lost.

ideas.name: The Household in Mourning
ideas.idea: When a standing character dies, every other standing character goes into mourning for it, for a term set by the dead one's level: one vigil per 10 levels, at least one. Full mourning is the first half of the term: the mourner earns 50% more Echoes and may not pick up coin. Half mourning is the second half: 25% more Echoes, coin allowed. A second death during the term extends it and does not stack. The death of a high character changes how the whole household plays for several vigils.
ideas.source: The length and grade of mourning depended on who had died, and the whole household wore it together.
ideas.nearest: Rested-experience bonuses. This is triggered by a death, scaled by what died, and comes with a rule about what may be picked up.

ideas.name: Told Out
ideas.idea: When a vigil ends, the bell tells the character out, and every stroke heard is one Echo. Tellers first: nine strokes if the character died, three if it left by a gate. Then one stroke for each character level, and one for each toll stood in that vigil. A death therefore pays six strokes more than an escape with the same record, and the death of a high character rings for a long time. The count is played in full, stroke by stroke, and can be listened to or skipped.
ideas.source: The death knell rang the tellers and then one stroke for each year of the dead person's age.
ideas.nearest: End-of-run currency tallies. This one is played as sound in the game's own code of strokes, and pays a fixed premium for dying.

ideas.name: Arrears
ideas.idea: A twist on one life and the tolls. Harm does not come off life when it lands. It is chalked on a slate as arrears. At each toll the slate is presented: life falls by the arrears and the slate is wiped. A character dies only at a toll, or at the instant arrears reach twice its remaining life. Between tolls arrears can be worked off: every experience pickup collected pays 1 point. The seconds before each bell are spent going back into the killing ground to pay.
ideas.source: A toll is both the stroke of a bell and a sum owed at a fixed point, and debts chalked on a slate fell due on a set day.
ideas.nearest: Delayed-damage pools cleared by a button, and regaining lost health by striking back quickly. Here one shared clock, the district bell, does all the collecting.

ideas.name: Abjuration
ideas.idea: A twist on one life. At no life a standing character need not die. Once in each district it may abjure: it is given a cross, its skills fall silent, and it has 40 s to walk the straight marked road to the nearest gate. The dead may jostle but not harm it; pushed or stepping more than 3 m off the road, it dies. Reaching the gate saves the character, but all it carries is forfeit and that district is closed to it for good.
ideas.source: A felon in sanctuary could save his life by abjuring the realm: walking straight to an assigned port with a cross, losing his goods and never returning.
ideas.nearest: Second-wind and last-stand rules. This buys the life with a permanent loss of territory, five times at most, and it has to be walked.

ideas.name: Tally at the Gate
ideas.idea: A twist on the gates. A gate offers two choices. Leave, banking everything as usual. Or split a tally and stay: half of what the character carries is banked now and is safe whatever happens; the gate keeps the stock and the character the foil. If the character later leaves alive by any gate in the same vigil, the halves are fitted and the half banked earlier is doubled. Only one tally can be open at a time. Dying with the foil loses the doubling, not the half.
ideas.source: With a split tally each party held half the record, and the bargain was completed when the halves were brought back together.
ideas.nearest: Safe-haven thresholds in quiz shows, and partial extraction. This adds a doubling that is paid only if the player also finishes alive.

ideas.name: A Wake for Your Dead
ideas.idea: A twist on the two ways to play. The one-sitting run through five districts is always a wake held for one of the player's dead standing characters, chosen at the start. The new character begins as that one's class with its first three picks already taken. Each district completed is one watch of the night. If all five are kept, the dead character's name goes on the bede-roll and whatever it left in the permanent tree gives double from then on. A broken wake may be held again.
ideas.source: A body was watched through the night before burial, and the names of the dead were entered on a bede-roll to be read aloud.
ideas.nearest: Run modes that revisit a past character's grave or ghost. Here the short mode exists to complete the long mode's deaths, and inherits their opening choices.

ideas.name: The Bell Tells What Comes
ideas.idea: A twist on the tolls. Each toll is not one stroke but a count. First the tellers: nine strokes if the coming 75 s will bring mostly large dead, six for middling, three for small and many. Then, after a pause, one quick stroke for each elite that will rise, and a single low stroke if a gate will open. A player who counts knows the next interval; one who does not is surprised by it. An option draws the count as marks, for play without sound.
ideas.source: Hearers of the death knell counted the tellers and the strokes of age to learn who had died before any news reached them.
ideas.nearest: Wave previews shown as icons. This puts the preview only in the synthesized bell, as a code the player learns to count.
